text:
Healthy sampled-negative margins do not establish strong full-catalog ranking. Krichene and Rendle show that sampled metrics can reverse model comparisons even in expectation; smaller candidate sets also obscure differences between ranking metrics ([KDD 2020](https://research.google/pubs/on-sampled-metrics-for-item-recommendation/)). Recent sequential-recommendation experiments find that aggregate accuracy hides head/mid/tail disparities: random training negatives favor head items, while popularity-based negatives can improve balance at an overall accuracy cost ([2024 study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.17276)). These findings support investigating popularity shortcuts, but do not establish that a particular BERT4Rec checkpoint uses them.

Suggested auxiliary audit: freeze exactly one BERT4Rec checkpoint per category; select a bounded, reproducible set of training-prefix/next-item pairs using training interactions only. Apply appended-mask inference, exclude prefix-seen items while retaining the target, and score the eligible catalog in chunks. Report target rank, catalog HR@10, and disagreement with 99-negative sampled hits. Repeat diagnostic sampling with uniform negatives and negatives matched to the target’s training-frequency bin; summarize rank variability and hit flips across draws, stratified by target popularity and history length. Frequency matching is a proposed control for easy popularity separation, not an unbiased relevance estimator.

For uncertainty, bootstrap users within each category, retaining their prefixes and candidate draws together; report paired diagnostic differences and equal-weight macro averages. Candidate resampling measures sampling sensitivity, while user resampling measures cohort uncertainty. Keep these training-recovery probes explicitly separate from generalization claims and the unchanged host validation HR@10; neither diagnostic candidate sets nor catalog metrics should replace the pinned selection criterion.
